subject: Science (IGCSE Biology, Chemistry, Physics)
board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9–1) Biology 4BI1, Chemistry 4CH1 and Physics 4PH1 (Science Double Award 4SD0 shares Papers 1B/1C/1P)
source: School Science curriculum journey 2026–27 (Year 10 Term 1: Chemistry Principles of Chemistry; Physics Forces and Motion) and the school's Year 10 Term 1 Week 2 Edexcel IGCSE Biology (4BI1) assessment on characteristics of living things, classification and cell biology; school 2024 papers 4BI1/1B, 4CH1/1C, 4PH1/1P for exam style; required practicals shown by demonstration for online delivery; INSET lesson standard.

lessons.unit: Biology: The nature and variety of living organisms
lessons.title: Characteristics of living organisms
lessons.bigQuestion: What exactly is the difference between living and non-living?
objectives: Recall the eight characteristics of living organisms used at IGCSE
Apply them to unfamiliar examples
Explain why viruses are a borderline case
successCriteria: List the characteristics in IGCSE wording
Apply them to decide whether something is living
Evaluate whether viruses are alive
lessons.crossCurricular: Islamic Studies: Al-Hayy (the Ever-Living); Chemistry: respiration as a chemical reaction
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: life as a gift and trust

keywords.def: taking in materials for energy, growth and development
chemical reactions that release energy from food
removal of toxic materials and waste products of metabolism
keeping internal conditions constant
detecting and responding to changes in the environment

starter: Bismillah. Recall MRS GREN from KS3

teach.heading: IGCSE characteristics
bullets: Eight characteristics used in the 4BI1 specification
teach.note: Contrast with KS3 MRS GREN: IGCSE adds control of internal conditions (homeostasis) and growth and development.

teach.heading: Excretion vs egestion
bullets: Excretion: waste made by metabolism (CO₂, urea)

misconception.wrong: Producing faeces is excretion
misconception.right: Faeces are egested; excretion removes metabolic waste like urea

teach.heading: Are viruses alive?
bullets: Not cells; protein coat and genetic material
teach.note: Answer the big question as a debate. Exam answers: viruses are not usually classed as living because they cannot carry out life processes outside a host.

check.q: Which is an example of excretion?
check.why: Urea is a metabolic waste product removed in urine. Faeces are egested; C is mainly temperature control.

practice: Why is a car not alive?
independent: Core: Write the IGCSE definition of each characteristic with a human example
Extend: Explain whether a plant seed in a packet is alive
Stretch: Exam question (4 marks): 'Viruses are not living organisms.' Evaluate this statement.
exit: Give one reason viruses are not considered living.
lessons.homework: Learn the eight characteristics; complete the retrieval quiz on the portal.
lessons.send: Support: definition cards. Stretch: prions and viroids.

lessons.unit: Biology: The nature and variety of living organisms
lessons.title: Plants, animals and fungi
lessons.bigQuestion: Why are mushrooms not plants?
objectives: Describe the features of plants, animals and fungi
Give named examples of each
Compare how they feed and store carbohydrate
successCriteria: Describe plants (maize, pea), animals (mammals, insects) and fungi (Mucor, yeast)
Compare cell features and carbohydrate stores
Classify unfamiliar organisms using these features
lessons.crossCurricular: Food technology: yeast in bread; Geography: biomes
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the variety of creation

keywords.def: cells with a nucleus
thread-like structures that make up a fungus
a network of hyphae
secreting enzymes onto food and absorbing the products
carbohydrate stored by animals and fungi

starter: Name two parts only in plant cells

teach.heading: Comparing three kingdoms
teach.note: Use 4BI1 named examples: maize, pea; mammals, insects; Mucor, yeast.

teach.heading: Saprotrophic nutrition
bullets: Food is digested outside the fungus

model.problem: Describe how Mucor feeds on bread (3 marks)
steps: They secrete enzymes that digest starch outside the hyphae
Soluble products (sugars) are absorbed into the hyphae

misconception.wrong: Mushrooms are plants because they don't move
misconception.right: Fungi lack chlorophyll and feed saprotrophically

check.q: An organism has hyphae, a chitin cell wall and stores glycogen. It is a…
check.why: Hyphae and chitin walls are fungal features. Plants have cellulose walls; animals have no walls.

practice: Name the carbohydrate stored by plants
independent: Core: Complete a comparison table of plants, animals and fungi
Extend: Explain why yeast is classed as a fungus even though it is single-celled
Stretch: 4BI1-style question: Explain why bread goes mouldy faster in a warm, damp kitchen.
exit: Name a plant example from the spec.
lessons.homework: Exam practice: 4BI1 Paper 1B-style questions on the variety of organisms (8 marks).
lessons.send: Support: comparison table frame. Stretch: lichens.

lessons.unit: Biology: The nature and variety of living organisms
lessons.title: Protoctists, bacteria, viruses and pathogens
lessons.bigQuestion: How can something too small to see kill a person?
objectives: Describe protoctists, bacteria and viruses
Give named examples from the specification
Define pathogen and name examples
successCriteria: Describe features of Chlorella, Amoeba, Lactobacillus and Pneumococcus
Describe the structure of viruses (influenza, HIV, tobacco mosaic virus)
Explain how pathogens cause disease, with examples
lessons.crossCurricular: History: pandemics and Ibn Sina's ideas on contagion; Food technology: Lactobacillus in yoghurt
lessons.smsc: Spiritual and moral: seeking cures (the hadith that Allah has sent a cure for every disease, Sahih al-Bukhari 5678)

keywords.def: a mostly microscopic eukaryotic organism, e.g. Amoeba
cells with no nucleus, e.g. bacteria
a small ring of DNA in bacteria
a protein coat around DNA or RNA; reproduces only inside host cells
a microorganism that causes disease

starter: Name the store of carbohydrate in animals
Name a disease caused by a virus

teach.heading: Bacteria
bullets: Cell wall, membrane, cytoplasm; some have flagella
teach.note: Lactobacillus: makes yoghurt. Pneumococcus: causes pneumonia.

teach.heading: Viruses
bullets: Not cells: protein coat with DNA or RNA
Examples: influenza, HIV, tobacco mosaic virus
teach.note: Answer the big question: viruses hijack cells and damage them as they multiply.

right.title: Virus
points: DNA or RNA in a protein coat

teach.heading: Pathogens
bullets: Can be fungi, bacteria, protoctists or viruses

misconception.wrong: Antibiotics cure the flu
misconception.right: Flu is viral; antibiotics only affect bacteria

check.q: Which organism has a plasmid and no nucleus?
check.why: Lactobacillus is a bacterium: prokaryotic, with plasmids. The others are eukaryotic.

practice: Describe the structure of a virus
Define pathogen and give two examples
independent: Core: Draw and label a bacterial cell
Extend: Compare a virus, a bacterium and a plant cell in a table
Stretch: 4BI1-style question (5 marks): Explain why antibiotics are not prescribed for colds, and why this matters.
exit: Name a bacterium in the spec.
Why aren't viruses killed by antibiotics?
Name a protoctist that causes disease.
lessons.homework: Complete the school's Term 1 Week 2 biology multiple-choice assessment (30 marks) and self-mark with the answer key.
lessons.send: Support: labelled diagrams. Stretch: virus replication cycle.

lessons.unit: Biology: Structures and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Levels of organisation and cell structure
lessons.bigQuestion: What do a leaf cell and a muscle cell have in common, and why?
objectives: Describe levels of organisation
Describe the structures in plant and animal cells and their functions
Compare plant and animal cells
successCriteria: Order organelle → organism
Describe the function of each cell structure
Explain the differences between plant and animal cells
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: reactions in the cytoplasm; Maths: magnification
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: order in creation

keywords.def: a specialised structure inside a cell
where proteins are made
site of aerobic respiration
site of photosynthesis
cellulose layer that supports plant cells

teach.heading: Levels of organisation
bullets: Organelles → cells → tissues → organs → organ systems

teach.heading: Cell structures
bullets: Know each structure and its job
teach.note: Answer the big question: both have nucleus, membrane, cytoplasm, mitochondria, ribosomes because all cells need control, exchange, reactions and energy.

head: Structure
Function
Plant
Animal
rows: contains genetic material; controls the cell

misconception.wrong: Mitochondria produce energy
misconception.right: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which releases energy

check.q: Which structure is found in both plant and animal cells?
check.why: Ribosomes make proteins in all cells. The others are plant-only.

practice: Three structures only in plant cells
independent: Core: Draw and label plant and animal cells with functions
Extend: Explain why root cells have no chloroplasts
Stretch: A cell from a muscle contains many more mitochondria than a skin cell. Explain why.
exit: Name the polysaccharide in plant cell walls.
lessons.homework: 4BI1 exam practice on cell structure (10 marks), including a labelled diagram question.
lessons.send: Support: labelled diagram templates. Stretch: magnification calculations.

lessons.unit: Biology: Structures and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Cell differentiation and stem cells
lessons.bigQuestion: If every cell has the same DNA, why are cells so different?
objectives: Explain cell differentiation
Describe stem cells in animals and plants
Evaluate the use of stem cells in medicine
successCriteria: Define differentiation and give examples
Compare embryonic and adult stem cells
Evaluate stem-cell treatments, including ethical issues
lessons.crossCurricular: Islamic Studies: Islamic bioethics and the sanctity of life; Medicine: transplants
lessons.smsc: Moral and spiritual: ethical debates on embryonic stem cells; differing scholarly views

keywords.def: a cell becoming specialised for a particular function
an undifferentiated cell that can divide and become specialised
can become almost any type of cell
plant tissue with stem cells, at root and shoot tips

teach.heading: Differentiation
bullets: All cells have the same genes

teach.heading: Stem cells
bullets: Plant meristems: any plant cell, throughout life

teach.heading: Evaluating stem-cell treatments
teach.note: Model a balanced answer. Mention that Muslim scholars hold differing views on embryonic stem-cell research; many permit research on surplus IVF embryos before a certain stage, others do not.

model.problem: Evaluate using stem cells to treat diabetes (4 marks)
steps: Benefit: could replace damaged insulin-producing cells
Risk: cells could divide uncontrollably (tumours) or be rejected
Ethical: embryonic sources are opposed by some on religious or moral grounds
model.answer: Benefits + risks + ethics, then a judgement

teach.heading: Same DNA, different cells
bullets: Cells don't lose genes when they specialise

misconception.wrong: Nerve cells contain only nerve genes
misconception.right: Every body cell has the full set of genes; only some are switched on

check.q: Where are stem cells found in plants?
check.why: Meristems at root and shoot tips contain dividing, unspecialised cells.

practice: Name a source of adult stem cells
independent: Core: Compare embryonic, adult and plant stem cells in a table
Extend: Explain why gardeners can grow new plants from cuttings
Stretch: Write a balanced 6-mark answer on whether embryonic stem-cell research should be allowed.
lessons.homework: Research one disease being treated with stem cells and summarise the treatment and its risks.
lessons.send: Support: comparison frame. Stretch: therapeutic cloning.

lessons.unit: Biology: Structures and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Biological molecules and food tests
lessons.bigQuestion: How can just a few chemical elements build every living thing?
objectives: Identify the elements in carbohydrates, proteins and lipids
Describe the structure of large biological molecules from smaller units
Describe practical food tests
successCriteria: State the chemical elements and building blocks of each molecule
Describe the four food tests including results
Interpret food test results in exam questions
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: elements and polymers; Food technology: nutrition
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: complexity built from simplicity

keywords.def: contains C, H and O; built from simple sugars
contains C, H, O and N; built from amino acids
contains C, H and O; built from fatty acids and glycerol
a large molecule made of repeating units

teach.heading: Building blocks
bullets: Large molecules are made from small units

teach.heading: Food tests (practical)
teach.note: Show demo video. 4BI1 asks for the method and result.

model.problem: Describe how to test a food for glucose (3 marks)
steps: Add Benedict's solution to a sample of the food in water
Heat in a water bath at about 80 °C for 5 minutes
A colour change from blue to green/yellow/orange/brick red shows glucose

teach.heading: Lipids are not polymers
bullets: Fatty acids + glycerol, not long chains of repeats
teach.note: A subtle point for top marks.

misconception.wrong: Lipids are polymers of fatty acids
misconception.right: A lipid is glycerol joined to three fatty acids: not a long repeating chain

check.q: Which element is in proteins but not in carbohydrates?
check.why: Amino acids contain nitrogen (in the amine group). Carbohydrates have only C, H and O.

independent: Core: Complete a food-test table for four nutrients (reagent, method, positive result)
Extend: Interpret results for three unknown foods
Stretch: Explain why a positive Benedict's result can be green or brick red, and how you could make the test more quantitative.
exit: How do you test for protein?
lessons.homework: 4BI1 Paper 1B-style questions on biological molecules and food tests.
lessons.send: Support: test cards. Stretch: semi-quantitative tests.

lessons.unit: Biology: Structures and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Enzymes: temperature and pH
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a high fever become dangerous?
objectives: Describe enzymes as biological catalysts
Explain the effect of temperature and pH on enzyme activity
Describe the practical investigation of temperature on enzyme activity
successCriteria: Explain lock and key and the active site
Explain the shape of temperature and pH graphs
Describe the amylase-starch practical with variables
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: catalysts and rates; Medicine: fever
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: precise balance (mizan) in the body

keywords.def: a protein that acts as a biological catalyst
the part of an enzyme where the substrate binds
the molecule an enzyme acts on
active site changed shape so substrate no longer fits
the condition at which an enzyme works fastest

teach.heading: Temperature
teach.note: Answer the big question: above about 40 °C, body enzymes begin to denature.

model.problem: Explain the shape of an enzyme activity–temperature graph (4 marks)
steps: As temperature rises, molecules have more kinetic energy
More successful collisions between enzyme and substrate
Peak at the optimum (about 37 °C for human enzymes)
Above it, bonds in the enzyme break, active site changes shape: denatured

teach.heading: pH
bullets: Each enzyme has an optimum pH
teach.note: Extremes of pH denature enzymes too.

teach.heading: Practical: amylase and temperature
bullets: Dependent: time for starch to disappear (iodine test)
teach.note: Show the demo video with a spotting tile.

misconception.wrong: Enzymes are killed at high temperatures
misconception.right: Enzymes are proteins, not alive; they are denatured

check.q: Why does activity fall above the optimum temperature?
options: The active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits
check.why: Heat breaks bonds holding the enzyme's shape, so the active site no longer matches the substrate.

practice: Name the dependent variable in the amylase practical
independent: Core: Sketch and explain temperature and pH graphs
Extend: Plan the amylase–temperature practical with variables, method and risk assessment
Stretch: Calculate the rate (1/time) from data at five temperatures and plot it.
exit: Why do enzymes work faster as temperature rises (below optimum)?
lessons.homework: 4BI1 practical-skills question on the enzyme investigation (method, variables, analysis).
lessons.send: Support: graph-sketch template. Stretch: rate calculations.

lessons.title: States of matter
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does steam scald worse than boiling water at the same temperature?
objectives: Describe the arrangement, movement and energy of particles in solids, liquids and gases
Describe changes of state using particle theory
Interpret heating and cooling curves
successCriteria: Draw and describe particles in each state
Name changes of state and explain them with forces and energy
Explain the flat sections of a heating curve
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: specific latent heat (Year 10 physics later); Geography: the water cycle
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: water in its three states as a sign (e.g. Surah An-Nur 24:43 on clouds and hail)

keywords.def: solid to liquid
solid directly to gas
forces between particles
a graph of temperature against time as a substance is heated

starter: Name the three states of matter
Why do solids keep their shape?

teach.heading: Particle model
bullets: Liquid: random, close, move past each other
teach.note: 4CH1 asks for arrangement, movement and relative energy.

teach.heading: Changes of state
teach.note: Answer the big question: steam releases extra energy when it condenses on your skin.

teach.heading: Heating curves
bullets: Energy breaks forces, not raising temperature

model.problem: Explain why the temperature stays at 0 °C while ice melts
steps: It is used to overcome forces between particles
Not to increase the particles' kinetic energy
So the temperature does not rise until all the ice has melted
model.answer: Energy goes into breaking forces of attraction

teach.heading: Particles don't change size
bullets: Particles themselves don't expand or melt

misconception.wrong: Particles get bigger when heated
misconception.right: Particles move faster and further apart; their size is unchanged

check.q: On a heating curve, what is happening during a flat section at 100 °C?
check.why: 100 °C is water's boiling point; the flat section is the liquid turning to gas.

practice: Name the change from gas to liquid
Why is there a flat section on a heating curve?
independent: Core: Label a heating curve for water from −20 °C to 120 °C
Extend: Explain sublimation of iodine using particle theory
Stretch: Use data to identify the state of five substances at 25 °C from their melting and boiling points.
exit: What happens to energy during melting?
lessons.homework: 4CH1 Paper 1C-style questions on states of matter.
lessons.send: Support: particle diagram templates. Stretch: data interpretation.

lessons.title: Diffusion and dilution
lessons.bigQuestion: How does the smell of oud spread across a whole room?
objectives: Explain diffusion using particle theory
Describe experiments showing diffusion and dilution
Explain why heavier gas particles diffuse more slowly
successCriteria: Describe diffusion in liquids and gases
Explain the ammonia and hydrogen chloride experiment
Explain dilution of potassium manganate(VII) as evidence for particles
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: diffusion in cells; Cultural studies: perfumes (attar) in Muslim cultures
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the sunnah of wearing perfume (for men) and the tradition of attar

keywords.def: net movement of particles from high to low concentration
adding solvent to make a solution less concentrated
sum of the relative atomic masses in a formula
how much solute is in a volume of solution

starter: Why can you smell cooking from another room?

teach.heading: Diffusion
bullets: Net movement from high to low concentration

teach.heading: Ammonia and hydrogen chloride
bullets: Cotton wool at each end of a tube
White ring of ammonium chloride forms
Ring is nearer the HCl end

model.problem: Explain why the white ring forms nearer the hydrogen chloride end
steps: NH₃ has Mr 17; HCl has Mr 36.5
NH₃ travels further in the same time
They meet nearer the HCl end

teach.heading: Dilution evidence
bullets: Potassium manganate(VII) dissolved, then diluted repeatedly
So the solid must be made of very many tiny particles

misconception.wrong: Particles diffuse because they want to spread out
misconception.right: Random motion produces a net movement from high to low concentration

check.q: Which gas diffuses fastest at the same temperature?
check.why: Lightest particles move fastest at a given temperature.

practice: Why is diffusion faster in gases?
What does the dilution experiment show?
independent: Core: Describe and explain the NH₃/HCl experiment with a diagram
Extend: Predict where the ring would form using hydrogen bromide (Mr 81) instead
Stretch: Explain how temperature affects the rate of diffusion, using particle energy.
exit: Why does NH₃ diffuse faster than HCl?
What does dilution show about particles?
lessons.homework: 4CH1 questions on diffusion experiments (6 marks).
lessons.send: Support: diagram labels. Stretch: Graham's law preview.

lessons.title: Elements, compounds, mixtures and separation
lessons.bigQuestion: How do chemists get pure substances from messy mixtures?
objectives: Distinguish elements, compounds and mixtures
Describe separation methods
Choose methods to separate mixtures
successCriteria: Classify substances
Describe simple and fractional distillation, filtration and crystallisation
Plan multi-step separations
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Jabir ibn Hayyan and the development of distillation; Geography: crude oil
lessons.smsc: Cultural: early chemists of the Islamic world who refined laboratory methods

keywords.def: a substance made of one type of atom
two or more elements chemically combined
substances not chemically combined
separating liquids with different boiling points using a fractionating column

starter: Is air an element, compound or mixture?

teach.heading: Element, compound, mixture
bullets: Mixture: no fixed ratio, not bonded
teach.note: Classify: O₂, H₂O, air, NaCl, sea water, Fe.

teach.heading: Fractional distillation
bullets: Column is hotter at the bottom
Lower boiling point liquid reaches the top first

model.problem: Explain how ethanol is separated from water
steps: Both evaporate; vapours rise up the fractionating column
Water condenses lower down and drips back
Ethanol vapour reaches the top and condenses in the condenser

teach.heading: Compound vs mixture
bullets: A compound has different properties from its elements

misconception.wrong: Salt water is a compound of salt and water
misconception.right: Salt water is a mixture: no new bonds between salt and water

check.q: Which method separates a mixture of two miscible liquids?
check.why: Miscible liquids have different boiling points; fractional distillation separates them.

practice: Method for pure water from ink?
independent: Core: Choose and explain methods for five mixtures
Extend: Plan how to get pure, dry salt from rock salt
Stretch: Explain why fractional distillation of crude oil works and why the fractions are still mixtures.
exit: Is brass an element, compound or mixture?
lessons.homework: 4CH1 separation questions including a diagram of fractional distillation.
lessons.send: Support: method decision flow. Stretch: crude oil fractions.

lessons.title: Paper chromatography
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a strip of paper prove a food colouring is safe?
objectives: Describe how to carry out paper chromatography
Calculate and use Rf values
Interpret chromatograms to identify substances
successCriteria: Describe the method including the pencil line
Calculate Rf values accurately
Use Rf and matching spots to identify components and impurities
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: ratio and division; Food technology: food additives
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest labelling and food safety

keywords.def: the result of chromatography
distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent
furthest point reached by the solvent
gives a single spot

starter: Why use pencil for labels on paper?

teach.heading: Method
bullets: Remove before the front reaches the top; mark it

teach.heading: Rf values
bullets: Measure to the centre of the spot
Same substance + same solvent = same Rf

model.problem: Spot at 3.9 cm, solvent front at 6.5 cm. Find Rf.

teach.heading: Interpreting

teach.note: Answer the big question: compare the food colouring with permitted dyes.

misconception.right: Spot ÷ solvent: Rf is always below 1

options: It is very likely pure A
check.why: One spot means one component; matching Rf in two solvents strongly suggests it is A.

practice: Why is the start line in pencil?
How many components in a 3-spot sample?
independent: Core: Calculate Rf for four spots and identify each from a reference table

Why must the solvent be below the line?

Use atomic number and mass number
Define isotopes
successCriteria: State relative mass and charge of protons, neutrons and electrons
Calculate numbers of subatomic particles
Explain what isotopes are with examples
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: radioactivity (later); History: models of the atom
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: Surah Saba 34:3, nothing 'the weight of an atom' escapes Allah's knowledge

keywords.def: positive particle in the nucleus, relative mass 1
neutral particle in the nucleus, relative mass 1
negative particle in shells, very small mass (about 1/1836)
number of protons
atoms of an element with different numbers of neutrons

starter: What charge does a proton have?

teach.heading: Subatomic particles
teach.note: Answer the big question: electrons in the outer parts of atoms repel each other.

model.problem: How many protons, neutrons and electrons in ²³Na (atomic number 11)?

Calculate Ar from isotope abundances
Explain why Ar is not a whole number
successCriteria: Define Ar relative to carbon-12
Calculate Ar from percentage abundances
Calculate an abundance from a given Ar

an average that accounts for how common each value is
the standard isotope used for atomic masses
